q: Photometry is the science of measuring visible light in units that are weighted according to the sensitivity of human eye.
e: True. Main quantities are luminous flux, intensity, luminance and illuminance. Photometry measures visible light with weights matched to the human eye, about 400 nm to 700 nm. Peak eye sensitivity is green near 555 nm.

q: The human eye responds only to light having wavelengths between about $400	ext{ nm}$ and $900	ext{ nm}$.
e: False. The human eye responds from about 400 nm to 700 nm, not out to 900 nm. 900 nm is infrared, which photometry of vision does not count. Green near 555 nm is the peak of that eye curve.

q: Human eye is more sensitive to green light of $555	ext{ nm}$ compared to other colors.
e: True. A different driver in place of Human would describe a different law. Human and eye have to stay with the same process.

q: In photometry, there are three main photometric quantities: luminous flux, luminous intensity, and illuminance.
e: False. Photometry also counts luminance, intensity per unit area in a given direction, as a main quantity. Flux, intensity, luminance, and illuminance are the set. Dropping luminance leaves the candela-per-square-metre idea out.

q: Luminous flux is a measurement of the power of visible light produced by a light source.
e: True. The eye's peak wavelength is why 555 nm is the luminous standard. Luminous flux is the visible-light power of a source, measured in lumen. One lumen is 1/683 watt at 555 nm, not at 400 nm.

q: Luminous flux is measured in lumen ($	ext{lm}$).
e: True. Luminous flux is the visible-light power of a source, measured in lumen. One lumen is 1/683 watt at 555 nm, not at 400 nm. The eye's peak wavelength is why 555 nm is the luminous standard.

q: One lumen is equivalent to $1/683	ext{ watt}$ of light with a wavelength of $400	ext{ nm}$.
e: False. One lumen is 1/683 watt of light at 555 nm, the eye's peak, not at 400 nm. 400 nm is the violet edge where the eye is much less sensitive. That 555 nm choice is why luminous units track vision.

q: Luminous intensity is a measure of the luminous flux emitted by a light source in a direction per unit solid angle.
e: True. Luminous intensity is flux per unit solid angle, I_v = Phi / Omega, in candela. Candela is lumen per steradian. Lux is illuminance, not this candela quantity.

q: Luminous intensity is measured in lux ($	ext{lx}$) or lumen per steradian.
e: False. Luminous intensity is the candela, lumen per steradian, not lux. Lux is illuminance, lumen per square metre. Steradian is a solid angle, not an area.

q: A solid angle is a measure of the amount of the field of view from some particular point that a given object covers.
e: True. In a solid, v = sqrt(Y/rho), Young's modulus over density. Y and the bulk modulus are elasticity properties, unit N m^-2. Liquids use bulk modulus B instead of Y.

q: In SI system, a solid angle is expressed in steradian ($	ext{sr}$).
e: True. In Delta U = Q - W, W is positive when the system does the work. Work done on the system is negative W in this convention. In a solid, v = sqrt(Y/rho), Young's modulus over density.

q: Luminance is the luminous intensity per unit area of light travelling in a given direction.
e: True. Lux is illuminance, not this candela quantity. Luminous intensity is flux per unit solid angle, I_v = Phi / Omega, in candela. Candela is lumen per steradian.

q: The SI unit for luminance is lux ($	ext{lx}$).
e: False. Luminance's SI unit is candela per square metre. Lux is illuminance on a receiving surface. Mixing those units mixes outgoing brightness with landing light.

q: Illuminance is the total luminous flux incident on a surface per unit area.
e: True. Illuminance is luminous flux landing per unit area, in lux, and follows E_v = I_v cos theta / r^2. It falls as the square of distance. School reading areas are often quoted near 500 lux.

q: The SI unit for illuminance is lux ($	ext{lx}$).
e: True. It falls as the square of distance. School reading areas are often quoted near 500 lux. Illuminance is luminous flux landing per unit area, in lux, and follows E_v = I_v cos theta / r^2.

q: The illuminance at any point on a surface is directly proportional to the square of the distance between the source and surface.
e: False. Illuminance is inversely proportional to the square of the source-to-surface distance. Double r and E_v falls to one quarter. A direct r squared law would brighten a surface as you walked away.
